pos: n. pl. (the bones, garments or possessions of a saint, kept and venerated as channels of grace)
etymology: Latin reliquiae, remains, from relinquere, to leave behind. Calvin's Treatise on Relics catalogued the trade and observed that the church had enough pieces of the true cross to freight a ship.
biblical_def: A relic is a physical remainder of a holy person kept for veneration. Scripture records two events the practice appeals to and neither establishes it: a dead man revived when he touched Elisha's bones (2Ki 13:21), a single unrepeated sign in a book of unrepeatable signs; and handkerchiefs from Paul's body healing the sick at Ephesus (Act 19:12), where the same chapter ends with the converts burning their magic books. Against the practice stands what Israel did with a genuine relic: Hezekiah “brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it” (2Ki 18:4). Moses' own grave was hidden, “but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day” (Deu 34:6). And at the empty tomb the question is, “Why seek ye the living among the dead?” (Luk 24:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines relics as the remains of the body of a saint; and, in a general sense, that which remains; that which is left after the loss or decay of the rest.
webster_full: RELIC, n. That which remains; that which is left after the loss or decay of the rest; as the relics of a town; the relics of a former generation.
2. The body of a deceased person; remains.
3. In the Romish church, the remains of the body of a saint, or something which belonged to a saint, preserved with great veneration as sacred memorials.
scriptures: And it came to pass, as they were burying a man, that, behold, they spied a band of men; and they cast the man into the sepulchre of Elisha: and when the man was let down, and touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet.
So that from his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out of them.

He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan.
And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Bethpeor: but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day.
And as they were afraid, and bowed down their faces to the earth, they said unto them, Why seek ye the living among the dead?
corruption_summary: A genuine object of God's own giving became an object of worship within a few centuries, and Hezekiah's response to it is in the canon.
corruption_paragraphs: The brasen serpent is the whole argument. God commanded Moses to make it, healing came through it, and the Lord Himself used it as a figure of His own lifting up. Seven hundred years later Israel was burning incense to it, and a godly king broke it in pieces and gave it a contemptuous name — Nehushtan, a piece of brass. The object was authentic and the veneration was still idolatry. That single verse answers every defence of relics built on the genuineness of the article, because 2 Kings 18:4 concerns an article no one could dispute.

Deuteronomy 34:6 is the positive design. The Lord buried Moses Himself in a valley in Moab, and no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day — a deliberate concealment of the grave of the greatest prophet Israel had, by the God who knew exactly what would have been built over it. Jude adds the strange detail that Michael contended with the devil about that body. Where God has hidden a thing, the church's business is not to go looking for it.

The medieval trade was a commercial industry with pilgrimage revenue attached, and Calvin's catalogue is devastating precisely because it is dry: he simply lists the churches and counts the duplicate heads, arms and nails. But the deeper objection is not fraud, which would be answered by better provenance. It is that the living Christ has given His church a table, a font, a Book and His own Spirit, and a congregation drawn to a bone has been drawn away from all four. Why seek ye the living among the dead?
roots_summary: Hebrew etsem (H6106), bone; nehushtan (H5180), a piece of brass; qeber (H6913), grave, sepulchre; Greek soudarion (G4676), handkerchief, napkin.
roots_lines: Hebrew etsem (H6106) — bone; 2 Kings 13:21, Genesis 2:23, Ezekiel 37:1–7.
Hebrew nehushtan (H5180) — Nehushtan, a thing of brass; 2 Kings 18:4 only — Hezekiah's contemptuous name for it.
Greek soudarion (G4676) — handkerchief, napkin; Acts 19:12, John 11:44, 20:7.
usage: “He brake in pieces the brasen serpent” — the article was genuine; the incense was not.
“No man knoweth of his sepulchre” — God hid the grave, and knew why.
“Why seek ye the living among the dead?” — asked at an empty tomb.

pos: n. (the act by which Rome declares a dead person a saint and directs that he be venerated)
etymology: From canon, a rule or list — to canonize is to enrol a name on the official list. The formal papal process dates from the tenth century; before that, local churches acclaimed their own martyrs.
biblical_def: Canonization enrols a dead believer among the saints by ecclesiastical decree. The New Testament's usage makes the category present-tense and congregation-wide: Paul writes “unto the church of God which is at Corinth, to them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints” (1Co 1:2) — to a church he then rebukes for incest, drunkenness at the table and lawsuits. Every epistle is addressed the same way: “to all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints” (Rom 1:7); “to the saints which are at Ephesus” (Eph 1:1); “the saints salute you” (2Co 13:13), written by the living to the living. The final judgment on any man's standing is reserved: “judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come” (1Co 4:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines canonization as the act of declaring a man a saint, or the ceremony of enrolling one in the catalogue of saints, called the canon.
webster_full: CANONIZATION, n. The act of declaring a man a saint, or rather the act of ranking a deceased person in the catalogue of saints, called a canon.
2. The state of being sainted.
CANONIZE, v.t. To declare a man a saint and enroll him in the canon or catalogue of saints.
scriptures: Unto the church of God which is at Corinth, to them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, with all that in every place call upon the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, both theirs and ours:
To all that be in Rome, beloved of God, called to be saints: Grace to you and peace from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, to the saints which are at Ephesus, and to the faithful in Christ Jesus:

Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts: and then shall every man have praise of God.
corruption_summary: Sainthood is made a posthumous rank for the exceptional, and Paul addressed it to a congregation with an incest case in it.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 1:2 is the verse that dismantles the whole apparatus, and its force is in the address. Paul calls these people sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints — and over the next sixteen chapters deals with a church split into factions, a man living with his father's wife, believers suing each other before pagan magistrates, and a Lord's table at which some went hungry while others got drunk. They are saints in the first verse and disgraceful in the fifth, because sainthood is a status conferred by Christ's work and not a grade earned by conduct. Take that away and every believer's assurance goes with it.

The corruption has a pastoral cost that outlives the doctrinal dispute. A church with an official class of saints will inevitably produce two tiers of Christian: the heroic few whose lives are extraordinary and the ordinary many who assume the promises are calibrated to the first group. The Protestant answer was not to abolish admiration for godly men — Hebrews 11 is a catalogue of them and Hebrews 13 says to follow their faith — but to deny that the difference is one of kind. The tinker in Bedford gaol and the ploughman and the mother are saints on the same ground as Augustine.

There is also the question of who may pronounce. First Corinthians 4:5 forbids the church to judge anything before the time, until the Lord come, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of the hearts — and a canonization is exactly a judgment of the counsels of a heart, delivered early, by men. The church may say a man's doctrine was sound and his life was fruitful; both are visible. Whether he stands is the Lord's to declare, and He has appointed a day for it.
roots_summary: Greek hagios (G40), holy, a saint; hagiazo (G37), to sanctify, set apart; kletos (G2822), called; kanon (G2583), a rule, measure.
roots_lines: Greek hagios (G40) — saint, holy one; used about sixty times of living believers; 1 Corinthians 1:2, Romans 1:7, Ephesians 1:1.
Greek kletos hagios (G2822 with G40) — called to be saints; Romans 1:7, 1 Corinthians 1:2 — the calling makes the saint.
Greek kanon (G2583) — rule, measure; Galatians 6:16, 2 Corinthians 10:13–16, Philippians 3:16.
usage: “Called to be saints” — written to the Corinthians, of all people.
“The saints salute you” — the living, greeting the living.
“Judge nothing before the time” — and a canonization is a judgment.

pos: n. and v. (a papal censure suspending the sacraments and public worship across a whole city or nation)
etymology: Latin interdicere, to forbid by decree. Innocent III laid England under interdict in 1208 for six years, closing the churches to force King John's hand.
biblical_def: An interdict withholds the ordinances from an entire population to coerce its ruler. Scripture's discipline is individual and remedial, aimed at recovery: the offender is dealt with privately, then before witnesses, then before the church, and only then treated as a heathen man and a publican (Mat 18:15–17); the incestuous man is delivered to Satan “that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus” (1Co 5:5), and when he repents the same apostle orders the church to “forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow” (2Co 2:7). The keys were given for building up: “whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Mat 16:19), and the authority is “for edification, and not for destruction” (2Co 10:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines interdict as a prohibition; and, in the Romish church, a prohibition of the pope, restraining the clergy from performing divine service, and depriving a whole kingdom of the sacraments.
webster_full: INTERDICT, v.t. To forbid; to prohibit; to debar.
2. To forbid or debar from communion; as, to interdict a prince or a nation.
INTERDICT, n. A prohibition; a prohibiting order or decree.
2. In the Romish church, a prohibition of the pope, by which the clergy are restrained from performing divine service, and the people deprived of the sacraments, in a whole kingdom, city or province.
scriptures: Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.
To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.
So that contrariwise ye ought rather to forgive him, and comfort him, lest perhaps such a one should be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow.
And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.
For though I should boast somewhat more of our authority, which the Lord hath given us for edification, and not for your destruction, I should not be ashamed:
corruption_summary: Church discipline is turned into a political weapon, and the people who lose the sacraments are the ones who did nothing.
corruption_paragraphs: The interdict inverts every feature of Matthew 18. There the discipline is personal — go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone; it escalates only on refusal; it aims at gaining a brother; and it ends with an individual, not a population. Under an interdict a farmer's child goes unbaptized and a widow is buried without a service because a king has offended a pope. The innocent are made hostages, which is the definition of a political instrument, and the ordinances of Christ are used as the leverage.

The corruption survives the institution that invented it. Whenever the Lord's table is withheld to enforce compliance in a matter Scripture has not made a term of communion — a building programme, a factional dispute, a pastor's wounded authority — the same inversion is at work in miniature. The test is 2 Corinthians 10:8: the authority was given for edification and not for destruction, and a discipline that has no path back into fellowship written into it has already failed the test. Second Corinthians 2:7 is the neglected half of the Corinthian case: the same church that put a man out is commanded to forgive and comfort him, lest he be swallowed up with overmuch sorrow. Discipline that cannot restore was never the church's kind.
roots_summary: Greek deo (G1210) and luo (G3089), to bind and to loose; ekklesia (G1577), church, assembly; oikodome (G3619), edification, building up; paradidomi (G3860), to deliver over.
roots_lines: Greek deo / luo (G1210, G3089) — bind and loose; Matthew 16:19, 18:18 — the keys, given to the church.
Greek oikodome (G3619) — edification; 2 Corinthians 10:8, 13:10, Ephesians 4:12, 4:29.
Greek paradidomi (G3860) — to deliver up; 1 Corinthians 5:5, 1 Timothy 1:20.
usage: “Between thee and him alone” — where discipline starts, and usually should end.
“That the spirit may be saved” — the purpose, even of the severest sentence.
“For edification, and not for destruction” — the test of any censure.

pos: n. (the doctrine that the whole Christ is present under either eucharistic species, used to justify withholding the cup from the laity)
etymology: Latin concomitari, to accompany. Defined at Constance in 1415, which conceded that Christ instituted the sacrament in both kinds and withheld the cup anyway.
biblical_def: Concomitance holds that because the living Christ is undivided, His blood accompanies His body under the bread, so the cup may be withheld from the people without loss. The institution is against it in the plainest words the Lord could have used: “he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it” (Mat 26:27); Mark records the obedience, “and they all drank of it” (Mar 14:23); Paul delivers the same rite to a Gentile church, “this cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:25), and states the double sign twice over: “as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines concomitance as a being together, or in connection with another thing; and concomitant as accompanying, conjoined with, concurrent.
webster_full: CONCOMITANCE, CONCOMITANCY, n. A being together or in connection with another thing.
CONCOMITANT, a. Accompanying; conjoined with; concurrent; attending.
CONCOMITANT, n. A companion; a person or thing that accompanies another, or is collaterally connected.
scriptures: And he took the cup, and gave thanks, and gave it to them, saying, Drink ye all of it;
And he took the cup, and when he had given thanks, he gave it to them: and they all drank of it.
After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me.
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
For I have received of the Lord that which also I delivered unto you, That the Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread:
corruption_summary: A clever inference is used to overturn a command, and the command was three words long.
corruption_paragraphs: The argument is not stupid. If Christ is risen and undivided, then wherever He is present He is wholly present, and the reasoning that follows from it is coherent. What the reasoning does is set aside Drink ye all of it — a direct imperative, spoken at the institution, with a word (all) that anticipates the very restriction later imposed. Mark notes that they all drank. Paul repeats the rite to a church far from that upper room and includes the cup each time he names the bread. When a theological inference, however tidy, ends by cancelling a plain command of the Lord about His own supper, the inference is what must give way.

The instinct underneath it is worth naming, because it is not confined to Rome: an anxiety about the people. The cup was withheld partly from fear of spillage, partly from a settled sense that the laity are a lesser order who may safely be given less. Every clericalism produces some version of that — a table fenced by the wrong criteria, a Bible effectively reserved to the trained, a worship in which the congregation watches. First Corinthians 11 was written to correct abuses at the table by putting the whole institution back into the hands of the whole church, which is what the apostle had received of the Lord and delivered unto them.
roots_summary: Greek poterion (G4221), cup; pino (G4095), to drink; diatheke (G1242), covenant, testament; anamnesis (G364), remembrance.
roots_lines: Greek poterion (G4221) — cup; Matthew 26:27, Mark 14:23, 1 Corinthians 10:16, 11:25–28.
Greek pinete ex autou pantes (G4095) — drink ye all of it; Matthew 26:27 — the imperative with pantes.
Greek anamnesis (G364) — remembrance; Luke 22:19, 1 Corinthians 11:24–25.
usage: “Drink ye all of it” — three words, and the doctrine sets them aside.
“And they all drank of it” — Mark records the obedience.
“As oft as ye drink it” — delivered to a Gentile church years later.

pos: adj. (pertaining to the pope or to the doctrines of the Roman church; the standard polemical adjective of the Reformation era)
etymology: From pope, Latin papa, father. The word is deliberately dismissive and appears throughout the Reformed confessions; the 1689 uses it once, of the doctrine of implicit faith.
biblical_def: Popish describes the doctrines and practices of Rome as the Reformers rejected them. The specific claims in view are answered directly: the title, “call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven” (Mat 23:9); the headship, for Christ “is the head of the body, the church… that in all things he might have the preeminence” (Col 1:18); the mediation, “for there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5); the authority of tradition, “laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men” (Mar 7:8); and the standing of every believer, “ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood” (1Pe 2:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines popish as relating to the pope; taught or ordained by the pope; pertaining to the Roman Catholic church, its doctrines and ceremonies.
webster_full: POPISH, a. Relating to the pope; taught or ordained by the pope; pertaining to the Roman Catholic church, or to the doctrines and ceremonies of that church.
POPERY, n. The doctrines and ceremonies of the Roman Catholic church.
scriptures: And call no man your father upon the earth: for one is your Father, which is in heaven.
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men, as the washing of pots and cups: and many other such like things ye do.
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
corruption_summary: The word became a slur that did the work of an argument, and the argument is the only part worth keeping.
corruption_paragraphs: This dictionary keeps the word because the confessions use it and a reader meeting it in Owen or the 1689 deserves to know what it means. It does not keep the habit that grew around it. Popish served for three centuries as a term that settled a question by naming it, so that a practice could be dismissed as popish without anyone showing from Scripture what was wrong with it — and by the eighteenth century the label was being applied to a written liturgy, a church calendar, a robe, a weekly communion, none of which is a doctrine at all. A word that spares a man the labour of argument will eventually replace his arguments.

The substantive disagreements are real and this entry names them without embarrassment: one Mediator, one Head, justification by an imputed righteousness received through faith alone, Scripture over tradition, a supper that is a remembrance and not a re-offering. Those are the issues the Reformation was about and they have not been resolved by anyone's good manners. But they must be argued as issues. A Protestant who cannot state Rome's actual position on justification before rejecting it is not defending the gospel; he is repeating a slogan, and the Ninth Commandment binds him in controversy as much as anywhere else.
roots_summary: Greek pater (G3962), father; kephale (G2776), head; mesites (G3316), mediator; paradosis anthropon (G3862), tradition of men.
roots_lines: Greek kephale (G2776) — head; Colossians 1:18, Ephesians 1:22, 5:23.
Greek mesites (G3316) — mediator; 1 Timothy 2:5, Hebrews 8:6, 9:15, 12:24 — always one.
Greek hierateuma basileion (G2406) — royal priesthood; 1 Peter 2:9, and hierateuma hagion, 2:5.
usage: “One is your Father, which is in heaven” — on the title.
“One mediator between God and men” — one, and He is named.
“A royal priesthood” — written to scattered laymen in Asia Minor.

pos: n. (a seat of judgment; a court, whether civil, ecclesiastical, or divine)
etymology: Latin tribunal, the raised platform on which a Roman magistrate's chair stood. The AV renders the same Greek word bema as judgment seat.
biblical_def: A tribunal is a bench from which judgment is given, and Scripture sets several of them one inside another. Pilate “sat down in the judgment seat in a place that is called the Pavement” (John 19:13), judging the Judge. Gallio “drave them from the judgment seat” at Corinth (Act 18:16). Above them all: “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad” (2Co 5:10); “we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ… every one of us shall give account of himself to God” (Rom 14:10–12). And the last court has no appeal: “I saw a great white throne, and him that sat on it” (Rev 20:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tribunal as the seat of a judge; the bench on which a judge and his associates sit for administering justice; and, more generally, a court of justice.
webster_full: TRIBUNAL, n. The seat of a judge; the bench on which a judge and his associates sit for administering justice.
2. More generally, a court of justice; as, the house of lords is the highest tribunal in Great Britain.
3. A judicatory; a bar.
scriptures: When Pilate therefore heard that saying, he brought Jesus forth, and sat down in the judgment seat in a place that is called the Pavement, but in the Hebrew, Gabbatha.
And he drave them from the judgment seat.
For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad.
But why dost thou judge thy brother? or why dost thou set at nought thy brother? for we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.
And I saw a great white throne, and him that sat on it, from whose face the earth and the heaven fled away; and there was found no place for them.
corruption_summary: Human courts are treated as final, and Scripture puts every one of them under a bench they will themselves stand before.
corruption_paragraphs: John 19:13 is one of the great ironies of the Passion and it is easy to read past. Pilate takes his seat on the bema, the official platform of Roman authority in Judea, and from it condemns a man who tells him plainly that he would have no power at all except it were given him from above. The Roman tribunal is real, its sentence is carried out, and it is sitting inside a larger courtroom the governor cannot see. That is the shape of every human judgment: genuinely authoritative, genuinely binding, and provisional.

The Christian consolation from this is not that verdicts do not matter but that they are not last. A man wrongly convicted, a pastor destroyed by a false report, an employee dismissed on a lie — each has a hearing coming at which the record is complete and the Judge cannot be misled. That is why Peter says of Christ that when He suffered He threatened not, but committed Himself to Him that judgeth righteously: not resignation but an appeal lodged in a higher court.

The warning runs the same direction and lands on believers first. Second Corinthians 5:10 says we must all appear, and Romans 14:10 puts it in a chapter about Christians despising each other over meat and days — the argument being that a man who will shortly stand before that bench has no business setting up his own. Every one of us shall give account of himself to God: himself, which is the clause that quietly ends most of the judging we do of each other.
roots_summary: Greek bema (G968), judgment seat, tribunal; krino (G2919), to judge; krima (G2917), judgment, sentence; thronos leukos (G2362), white throne.
roots_lines: Greek bema (G968) — judgment seat; John 19:13, Acts 18:12–17, 25:10, Romans 14:10, 2 Corinthians 5:10.
Greek krino (G2919) — to judge; Romans 14:3–13, John 5:22, Acts 17:31.
Greek thronos (G2362) — throne; Revelation 20:11, 4:2, Hebrews 4:16 — the same seat is a throne of grace first.
usage: “Pilate… sat down in the judgment seat” — a court inside a larger court.
“We must all appear” — all, and it is said to the church.
“Every one of us shall give account of himself” — of himself, which ends most quarrels.

pos: n. (a forbidding by authority; a rule that a thing not be done)
etymology: Latin prohibere, to hold back, from habere, to hold. In American usage the word carries the memory of the Eighteenth Amendment, which is a useful case rather than a distraction.
biblical_def: A prohibition forbids. Scripture is full of divine ones and warns sharply about invented ones: “Touch not; taste not; handle not; which all are to perish with the using; after the commandments and doctrines of men” (Col 2:21–22), rules that have “a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh” (Col 2:23). Paul names as a doctrine of devils the “forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving” (1Ti 4:3). Yet real prohibitions bind — “abstain from all appearance of evil” (1Th 5:22) — and liberty is never a licence: “all things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient” (1Co 6:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prohibition as the act of forbidding or interdicting; a declaration to hinder some action; an interdict.
webster_full: PROHIBITION, n. The act of forbidding or interdicting; a declaration to hinder some action; interdict.
2. In law, a writ of prohibition is a writ issuing from a superior tribunal, directed to the judges of an inferior court, commanding them to cease from the prosecution of a suit.
scriptures: Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.
Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth.
Abstain from all appearance of evil.
All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any.
corruption_summary: Man-made rules are added to God's and enforced harder than His, because they are easier to keep and easier to measure.
corruption_paragraphs: Colossians 2:23 is the most uncomfortable sentence in the New Testament for the rule-making temperament: such regulations have a shew of wisdom — they look godly, they cost something, they produce visible restraint — and they are not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh. They do not work. A prohibition can stop a hand and cannot touch an appetite, and the man who keeps it may simply have relocated his sin somewhere the rule does not reach. Meanwhile the rule furnishes him with grounds for confidence, which is the worse outcome, because the flesh is nourished by successful abstinence as readily as by indulgence.

The reason churches drift into man-made prohibitions is that they are administrable. Love your wife as Christ loved the church cannot be audited; a dress code can. Be angry and sin not is a lifetime's work; a ban on a beverage can be signed. Congregations reach for the enforceable proxy in good faith and then, within a generation, the proxy has become the boundary of fellowship — and 1 Timothy 4:3 shows how far that road runs, since forbidding marriage and meats is called a doctrine of devils, not a harmless excess of zeal.

None of this dissolves the real prohibitions, and the abuse of the category is no argument against its use. God forbids a great deal, plainly, and 1 Corinthians 6:12 gives the mature form of the liberty that remains: all things are lawful, but not all expedient, and Paul adds that he will not be brought under the power of any. The Christian is freed from the commandments of men in order to be governed by conscience under Scripture — a heavier yoke in practice than a rule-book, and the only one that reaches the appetite.
roots_summary: Greek dogmatizo (G1379), to be subject to ordinances; ethelothreskeia (G1479), will worship; koluo (G2967), to forbid, hinder; exestin (G1832), it is lawful.
roots_lines: Greek dogmatizo (G1379) — to submit to ordinances; Colossians 2:20 only.
Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479) — will worship, self-chosen religion; Colossians 2:23 only.
Greek koluo (G2967) — to forbid; 1 Timothy 4:3, Matthew 19:14, Acts 10:47.
usage: “Touch not; taste not; handle not” — quoted by Paul as the words of others.
“A shew of wisdom… not in any honour” — they look godly and do not work.
“All things are lawful… but I will not be brought under the power of any”.

pos: adj. (original; belonging to the first age; of the earliest church, before later additions)
etymology: Latin primitivus, first of its kind, from primus, first. “The primitive church” was the Reformers' standing appeal — not to antiquity as such but to the apostolic pattern.
biblical_def: Primitive means first, original, belonging to the beginning. The apostolic pattern is set down plainly: “they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42). The appeal to it is a prophetic instinct: “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls” (Jer 6:16). Jude urges believers “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3). The Lord Himself settles a marriage question by going behind Moses: “but from the beginning it was not so” (Mat 19:8). And Ecclesiastes warns against a merely nostalgic version (Ecc 7:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines primitive as pertaining to the beginning or origin; original; first; and, of the church, ancient, as in the primitive fathers.
webster_full: PRIMITIVE, a. Pertaining to the beginning or origin, or to early times; original; first; as primitive innocence; the primitive church.
2. Formal; affectedly solemn; imitating the supposed gravity of old times.
3. Original; primary; radical; not derived; as a primitive word.
scriptures: And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
He saith unto them, Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.
Say not thou, What is the cause that the former days were better than these? for thou dost not enquire wisely concerning this.
corruption_summary: The appeal to the first age becomes nostalgia for a church that never existed, and Corinth was a primitive church too.
corruption_paragraphs: The Reformed appeal to the primitive church is legitimate and it has a precise form: what the apostles taught and instituted binds, what later ages added does not. It is not an appeal to antiquity in general — error is also ancient, and the New Testament epistles are largely occupied with first-century error. The moment the argument becomes older is purer it has left its footing, because Galatians was written to a first-generation church that had already lost the gospel, and Revelation 2 addresses a church of the apostolic age that had left its first love.

The sentimental version does real damage in congregations. A church imagining Acts 2 as an unbroken idyll of shared meals and daily miracles will read its own ordinary difficulties as decline, and Acts itself refuses the picture: the widows were neglected in the daily ministration, Ananias lied, Paul and Barnabas parted asunder, and the Jerusalem council existed because there was a dispute serious enough to need one. Ecclesiastes 7:10 names the mood exactly — say not thou, What is the cause that the former days were better than these? for thou dost not enquire wisely concerning this.

Jeremiah 6:16 gives the sound version, and its last clause is the point. Ask for the old paths, where is the good way — the old path is commended because it is good, not merely because it is old, and the two adjectives are both doing work. The verse ends badly: but they said, We will not walk therein. The danger for the antiquarian is that a man may locate the old path with great scholarly precision and decline to walk on it, which is a more sophisticated failure than the one Jeremiah was addressing and lands in the same place.
roots_summary: Greek arche (G746), beginning; hapax paradotheise (G530, G3860), once delivered; Hebrew olam (H5769), ancient, of old; nethibah (H5410), path.
roots_lines: Greek arche (G746) — beginning; Matthew 19:4–8, John 1:1, 1 John 1:1, 2:7.
Greek hapax (G530) — once for all; Jude 1:3, Hebrews 9:26–28, 10:10.
Hebrew nethiboth olam (H5410 with H5769) — the old paths; Jeremiah 6:16, 18:15.
usage: “They continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine” — the pattern, in one verse.
“Ask for the old paths, where is the good way” — old and good, both required.
“What is the cause that the former days were better?” — thou dost not enquire wisely.

pos: n. (uprightness of principle; straightness of character; conformity to the rule of right)
etymology: Latin rectitudo, straightness, from rectus, straight — the same root as right and rule. The moral word is a builder's word: a thing is upright when it matches the line.
biblical_def: Rectitude is moral straightness — a life that answers to the line. It is how man was made: “God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions” (Ecc 7:29). It is what God is: “a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he” (Deu 32:4). It is what He looks for: “the LORD trieth the righteous”, and “his countenance doth behold the upright” (Psa 11:5–7). It is Job's character before the accusation, “perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil” (Job 1:1). And it is a possession worth more than an argument: “the integrity of the upright shall guide them” (Pro 11:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rectitude as, in morality, rightness of principle or practice; uprightness of mind; exact conformity to truth, or to the rules prescribed for moral conduct.
webster_full: RECTITUDE, n. Literally, straightness; but in this sense not used.
2. In morality, rightness of principle or practice; uprightness of mind; exact conformity to truth, or to the rules prescribed for moral conduct, either by divine or human laws.
Rectitude of mind is the disposition to act in conformity to any known standard of right, truth or justice.
scriptures: Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions.
He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he.
For the righteous LORD loveth righteousness; his countenance doth behold the upright.
There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job; and that man was perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil.
The integrity of the upright shall guide them: but the perverseness of transgressors shall destroy them.
corruption_summary: Rectitude is confused with reputation, and a straight man may be universally thought crooked.
corruption_paragraphs: Job is the canonical case and the book exists partly to keep the two apart. He is declared perfect and upright by God in chapter one, and for thirty-five chapters his friends explain to him that his suffering proves he is not — a theology of reputation, in which the visible outcome reveals the hidden character. Job's refusal to confess sins he had not committed, merely to make his misery intelligible to his comforters, is itself an act of rectitude and looks to everyone in the room like pride. A man may be straight and be measured by a bent rule.

The opposite error is commoner in our own time and it is subtler: sincerity substituted for straightness. Rectitude is conformity to a standard outside the self, which is why Webster's definition is worth the whole entry — exact conformity to truth, or to the rules prescribed for moral conduct. Being true to oneself is not in the definition anywhere. Ecclesiastes 7:29 is exact about what went wrong: God made man upright, and the ruin came through many inventions, which is to say through men supplying their own standard.

Proverbs 11:3 gives the practical benefit and it is not the one usually advertised. The integrity of the upright shall guide them — rectitude functions as a compass, not merely as a credential. The man who has settled in advance that he will not lie has removed most of the hard decisions from his week; the man who has kept the question open must relitigate it under pressure every time, and pressure is exactly the condition under which no one judges well. Half of practical wisdom is a decision made early enough that it is no longer a decision.
roots_summary: Hebrew yashar (H3477), straight, upright; tom / tummah (H8537, H8538), integrity, completeness; tam (H8535), perfect, blameless; tsaddiq (H6662), just, righteous.
roots_lines: Hebrew yashar (H3477) — upright, straight; Ecclesiastes 7:29, Deuteronomy 32:4, Psalm 11:7, 33:1.
Hebrew tam (H8535) — perfect, complete; Job 1:1, 1:8, 2:3 — God's own word for him.
Hebrew tummah (H8538) — integrity; Proverbs 11:3, Job 2:3, 2:9, 27:5.
usage: “God hath made man upright” — and the ruin came by inventions.
“Perfect and upright” — God's assessment, before the comforters gave theirs.
“The integrity of the upright shall guide them” — a compass, not a credential.

pos: n. pl. (natural gifts of mind or person; also, property settled on a church or institution for its permanent support)
etymology: From endow, Old French douer, Latin dotare, to give a dowry. The word holds both senses at once: what a man is given in himself, and what is given to keep an institution standing.
biblical_def: Endowments are gifts bestowed — abilities in a man, or goods settled on an institution. Scripture treats the first as wholly derived: “what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?” (1Co 4:7). They are distributed unequally by design, “to every man according to his several ability” (Mat 25:15), and the gifts are “differing according to the grace that is given to us” (Rom 12:6). Their purpose is not display: “as every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1Pe 4:10). And more given means more required: “unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required” (Luk 12:48).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines endowment as the act of settling a fund or permanent provision for the support of an institution; and, in the plural, that which is given or bestowed on the person or mind by the creator; gifts of nature.
webster_full: ENDOWMENT, n. The act of settling dower on a woman.
2. The act of settling a fund or permanent provision for the support of a public institution.
3. That which is bestowed or settled on a person or an institution; property, fund or revenue permanently appropriated to any object.
4. That which is given or bestowed on the person or mind by the creator; gifts of nature; any quality or faculty.
scriptures: For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it?
And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey.
Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of faith;
As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.

But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes. For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: and to whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more.
corruption_summary: Gifts are mistaken for merit, and an institution's endowment outlives the convictions it was raised to defend.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 4:7 puts three questions in a row and the third is the one that lands: who maketh thee to differ? what hast thou that thou didst not receive? and if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory as if thou hadst not received it? Note the last clause — the boasting proceeds as if the gift were not a gift. Almost nobody denies that his intelligence or voice or nerve came from somewhere; the pride is in the forgetting rather than the denying, and it is nearly automatic. The parable of the talents keeps the same accounting: the sums differ, the servants own none of them, and the reckoning is about use rather than amount.

The institutional sense carries its own decay and church history is full of it. A fund is settled to train ministers in sound doctrine; the doctrine is abandoned within a century and the fund remains, now paying the salaries of men who teach the opposite, because money is easier to entail than conviction. The lesson is not that endowments are wrong — the Levites were provided for, and Paul says they that preach the gospel should live of the gospel — but that no charter can substitute for living faith in the next generation. An institution is only ever one generation from losing what it was built to keep.

Luke 12:48 balances the ledger and is worth setting beside the envy that endowments provoke. Unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required — the gifted man's advantage is real and so is the weight on it, and he is not to be envied so much as prayed for. The Reformed doctrine of vocation follows: the question is never whether a man's gifts are large but whether they are being spent on what he was given them for, and the servant with two talents and the servant with five hear precisely the same commendation.
roots_summary: Greek charisma (G5486), gift of grace; lambano (G2983), to receive; dunamis (G1411), ability, power; oikonomos (G3623), steward.
roots_lines: Greek charisma (G5486) — a gift of grace; Romans 12:6, 1 Corinthians 12:4, 1 Peter 4:10.
Greek dunamis (G1411) — ability, power; Matthew 25:15 — according to his several ability.
Greek oikonomos (G3623) — steward; 1 Peter 4:10, 1 Corinthians 4:1–2, Titus 1:7.
usage: “What hast thou that thou didst not receive?” — and the glorying is in the forgetting.
“According to his several ability” — unequal by design.
“Of him shall be much required” — the weight that comes with the gift.
